decks.title: Peasants, Zamindars and the State — Part 1: Peasants, the Ain and the Village
goals: Describe peasants, their holdings, farming, seasons and crops in the Mughal countryside
Explain what the Ain-i Akbari is, and judge its strengths and limits as a source
Describe the village community, caste, artisans and the position of women
Plan a 5-mark answer, read crop figures and read a petition

slides.heading: Peasants, Zamindars and the State
slides.body_md: Part 1: **peasants**, the **Ain-i Akbari** and the **village community**.

visual.alt: Flow chart, Part 1 at a glance: Peasants and farming, then The Ain-i Akbari, then The village community, then Caste, artisans and women
visual.caption: Part 1 at a glance

slides.narration: In the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, most people of the Mughal empire lived by farming. In this part we meet the peasants, learn how historians use the Ain of Akbar as a source, and then look inside the village, at its elders, its castes, its artisans and its women.

slides.heading: Who were the peasants?
slides.body_md: Several words described those who farmed: **raiyat** and **muzarian**, and **kisan** or **asami**.

rows: Cultivator living in the village where he held land
Non-resident cultivator who cultivated land elsewhere

visual.alt: Table, Terms for peasants. Raiyat (riaya) or muzarian: A peasant; Kisan or asami: Other words for a cultivator; Khud-kashta: Cultivator living in the village where he held land; Pahi-kashta: Non-resident cultivator who cultivated land elsewhere
visual.caption: Terms for peasants

slides.narration: Sources of the time call a peasant a raiyat, or muzarian, and also a kisan or asami. Some peasants were khud kashta, living in the village where they held land. Others were pahi kashta, non resident cultivators who farmed land elsewhere, often because the terms were better or because they had moved.

slides.heading: Land plentiful, labour scarce
slides.body_md: When land is plentiful and hands are few, peasants can **move** to better terms.

visual.alt: Flow chart, Why peasants moved: Land was plentiful, then Labour was scarce, then Peasants moved to better terms
visual.caption: Why peasants moved

slides.narration: Land was abundant and labour was scarce. That is why peasants could move, and why the pahi kashta existed. Holdings were modest. In north India an average peasant seldom had more than a pair of bullocks and two ploughs, while in Gujarat a peasant with about six acres was counted as well off.

slides.heading: Quick check: a term
slides.body_md: Which pair of terms was commonly used for a peasant?
slides.narration: Recall the terms for a peasant.

slides.heading: Water for the fields
slides.body_md: Farming rested on the **monsoon**, helped by wells, tanks and canals.

rows: Raised water; the Persian wheel was used in some regions
Built or repaired, sometimes by the state, as the Shah Nahr in the Punjab under Shah Jahan

visual.alt: Table, Water for the fields. Rain: Agriculture depended on the monsoon; Wells: Raised water; the Persian wheel was used in some regions; Tanks and canals: Built or repaired, sometimes by the state, as the Shah Nahr in the Punjab under Shah Jahan
visual.caption: Water for the fields

slides.narration: Agriculture depended on the monsoon, but farmers also drew water from wells and tanks, and used canals. In some regions the Persian wheel raised water. The state sometimes built or repaired canals, for example the Shah Nahr in the Punjab under Shah Jahan, which shows that irrigation was not only a village matter.

slides.heading: Seasons and crops
slides.body_md: Two harvests, many crops, **cash crops** and **new arrivals** from the Americas.

rows: Agra 39 kinds of crop and Delhi 43 over the two seasons; Bengal 50 varieties of rice
Cash crops such as cotton and sugarcane; also oilseeds and lentils
Maize; tomatoes, potatoes and chillies; pineapple and papaya

visual.alt: Table, Seasons and crops. Two seasons: Kharif (autumn) and rabi (spring); Variety in the Ain: Agra 39 kinds of crop and Delhi 43 over the two seasons; Bengal 50 varieties of rice; Jins-i kamil: Cash crops such as cotton and sugarcane; also oilseeds and lentils; From the Americas: Maize; tomatoes, potatoes and chillies; pineapple and papaya
visual.caption: Seasons and crops

slides.narration: There were two seasons, kharif in autumn and rabi in spring. The Ain says that Agra grew thirty nine kinds of crop and Delhi forty three over the two seasons, and Bengal had fifty varieties of rice alone. Cash crops such as cotton and sugarcane were called jins i kamil. Maize, tomatoes, chillies and pineapple came from the Americas.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: reading crop figures
slides.body_md: Imagined village: *150 bighas in all; 30 under cotton and 24 under sugarcane.*
bullets: Step 2 — Find the **share** of the total.

rows: 30 bighas of cotton and 24 of sugarcane make 54 bighas
About a third of the land was grown for sale
How much was sold, to whom and at what price

visual.alt: Table, Reading crop data. Cash crops: 30 bighas of cotton and 24 of sugarcane make 54 bighas; Share: 54 of 150 is 36 per cent; Reading: About a third of the land was grown for sale; Missing: How much was sold, to whom and at what price
visual.caption: Reading crop data

slides.narration: Take an imagined village of one hundred and fifty bighas. Thirty bighas of cotton and twenty four of sugarcane make fifty four, which is thirty six per cent of the land. So about a third was grown for sale. But the figures do not show how much was sold, to whom, or at what price, so we must not claim that the peasants gained.

slides.heading: The Ain-i Akbari
slides.body_md: Written by **Abu'l Fazl** and completed in **1598**, after five revisions.

rows: To present an empire whose ruling class ensured social harmony

visual.alt: Table, The Ain-i Akbari. Author: Abu'l Fazl, Akbar's court historian; Completed: 1598, after five revisions; Place: Third part of the Akbarnama; Aim: To present an empire whose ruling class ensured social harmony
visual.caption: The Ain-i Akbari

slides.narration: The Ain i Akbari was written by Abu l Fazl, the court historian of Akbar, and completed in fifteen ninety eight after five revisions. It is the third part of the Akbarnama. Its aim was to present an empire with a ruling class that ensured social harmony, so it is a source with a point of view.

slides.heading: Quick check: author and date
slides.body_md: The Ain-i Akbari was written by ___, the court historian of Akbar, and was completed in ___.
slides.narration: Recall the author and the year.

slides.heading: What the Ain contains

rows: Military and civil administration, nobles and servants
The fiscal side: revenue rates and the Account of the Twelve Provinces
Religious, literary and cultural traditions; Akbar's auspicious sayings

visual.alt: Table, The five books of the Ain. 1. Manzil-abadi: The imperial household; 2. Sipah-abadi: Military and civil administration, nobles and servants; 3. Mulk-abadi: The fiscal side: revenue rates and the Account of the Twelve Provinces; 4 and 5: Religious, literary and cultural traditions; Akbar's auspicious sayings
visual.caption: The five books of the Ain

slides.narration: The Ain has five books. The first three describe the administration: the imperial household, the military and civil administration, and the fiscal side, which includes revenue rates and the Account of the Twelve Provinces. The fourth and fifth books deal with the religious, literary and cultural traditions of the people and with a collection of Akbar auspicious sayings.

slides.heading: Strengths and limits of the Ain
slides.body_md: Extraordinarily valuable, yet with **errors** and **uneven data**.

rows: Data not collected evenly: caste of zamindars missing for some provinces, fiscal data for others
Largely from Agra and its surroundings

visual.alt: Table, Strengths and limits of the Ain. An extraordinary range of statistics: Errors in totalling; Detailed account of provinces: Data not collected evenly: caste of zamindars missing for some provinces, fiscal data for others; Prices and wages: Largely from Agra and its surroundings
visual.caption: Strengths and limits of the Ain

slides.narration: The Ain is extraordinarily valuable for its range of statistics. But it has errors in totalling, and its data were not collected evenly from every province. For some provinces the caste of zamindars is missing, for others fiscal data. Prices and wages come largely from Agra and its surroundings. So a careful historian checks the Ain against other records.

visual.caption: The village community and its officials

slides.narration: The village community had three constituents: the cultivators, the panchayat and the headman. The headman, called muqaddam or mandal, was chosen by consensus and approved by the zamindar. He kept the accounts with the help of the patwari. The panchayat was an assembly of elders. Cultivators came from many castes, with deep inequalities among them.

slides.heading: What the panchayat did
slides.body_md: A **common fund**, **fines** and **expulsion**; it kept caste boundaries.

rows: Chosen by consensus, approved by the zamindar; kept accounts with the patwari
Assembly of elders, usually heads of families; a common fund; fines and expulsion

visual.alt: Table, Village roles. Headman: Chosen by consensus, approved by the zamindar; kept accounts with the patwari; Panchayat: Assembly of elders, usually heads of families; a common fund; fines and expulsion; Cultivators: Khud-kashta and pahi-kashta
visual.caption: Village roles

slides.narration: The panchayat was usually made up of heads of families, with representatives of different castes in mixed villages, though the powerful dominated it. It had a common fund from contributions. It ensured that caste boundaries were kept, and it could impose fines and order expulsion. In Rajasthan, caste panchayats also arbitrated disputes.

slides.heading: Caste, artisans and the little republic
slides.body_md: Inequality was deep; artisans were paid in **shares** or **plots**.

rows: On the margins; among Muslim communities the halalkhoran were housed outside the village
Paid with a share of the harvest, a plot, or both; the plot was miras or watan in Maharashtra

visual.alt: Table, Caste and artisans. Menial labourers: On the margins; among Muslim communities the halalkhoran were housed outside the village; Mallahzadas in Bihar: Recorded as comparable to slaves; Artisans: Paid with a share of the harvest, a plot, or both; the plot was miras or watan in Maharashtra
visual.caption: Caste and artisans

slides.narration: Caste inequalities were deep. Menial labourers lived on the margins, and among Muslim communities the halalkhoran were housed outside the village. In Bihar, the mallahzadas are recorded as comparable to slaves. Artisans such as potters and blacksmiths were paid with a share of the harvest or a plot. British officials called villages little republics, but historians question the term.

slides.heading: Women in agrarian society
slides.body_md: Women **worked** in the fields and crafts, and could **petition** the panchayat.

rows: Sowing, weeding, threshing and winnowing; spinning, sieving, clay, embroidery
Bride-price common; remarriage of divorced and widowed women legitimate
Women of the landed gentry could inherit; a woman held the Rajshahi zamindari in the 18th century

visual.alt: Table, Women in agrarian society. Work: Sowing, weeding, threshing and winnowing; spinning, sieving, clay, embroidery; Marriage: Bride-price common; remarriage of divorced and widowed women legitimate; Household: Men controlled it; Redress: Women petitioned panchayats; Property: Women of the landed gentry could inherit; a woman held the Rajshahi zamindari in the 18th century
visual.caption: Women in agrarian society

slides.narration: Women worked alongside men in sowing, weeding, threshing and winnowing, and also in spinning, sieving, clay work and embroidery. Because their labour was valued, bride price rather than dowry was common, and remarriage of divorced and widowed women was legitimate. Men controlled the household, yet women petitioned panchayats. Women of the landed gentry could inherit property.

decks.title: Peasants, Zamindars and the State — Part 2: Forests, Zamindars, Revenue and Silver
goals: Explain how forest dwellers, the state and trade affected one another
Describe zamindars: their land, revenue role, forces and relation with peasants
Explain the land revenue system, its terms, land classes and the mansabdari link
Explain the flow of silver and weigh how far it explains cash revenue

slides.heading: Forests, Zamindars, Revenue and Silver
slides.body_md: Part 2: **forests and tribes**, **zamindars**, **land revenue** and the **flow of silver**.

visual.alt: Flow chart, Part 2 at a glance: Forests and tribes, then Zamindars, then Land revenue, then The flow of silver
visual.caption: Part 2 at a glance

slides.narration: In this part we leave the village for the forest and the fort. We meet forest peoples and the state, then the zamindars, who held land and collected revenue. Then we study how the empire raised its revenue, and how silver from the wider world helped it to do so in cash.

slides.heading: Forest peoples and the state
slides.body_md: **Jangli** described a way of living; the state wanted **elephants**.

rows: Forest produce, hunting and shifting cultivation
Described a way of living, not savagery
Shikar was described by the court as an occasion to dispense justice

visual.alt: Table, Forest dwellers. Livelihood: Forest produce, hunting and shifting cultivation; The word jangli: Described a way of living, not savagery; State demand: Elephants, supplied as peshkash; Hunts: Shikar was described by the court as an occasion to dispense justice
visual.caption: Forest dwellers

slides.narration: In Mughal usage, jangli meant people whose livelihood came from forest produce, hunting and shifting cultivation. It described a way of living, not savagery. The state needed elephants and asked forest peoples to supply them as peshkash, a form of tribute. Court writers described imperial hunts as occasions to dispense justice.

slides.heading: Trade changes forest societies
slides.body_md: Trade in **honey**, **beeswax** and **gum lac** helped some chiefs to rise.

visual.alt: Flow chart, How trade changed forest societies: Honey, beeswax, gum lac, then Carried to distant markets, then Chiefs gain wealth and power, then Some become zamindars or kings
visual.caption: How trade changed forest societies

slides.narration: Forest produce such as honey, beeswax and gum lac was carried to distant markets. Changes in forest societies came through trade, through the demands of the state, and through social factors. Some forest chiefs became zamindars, and in Assam the Koch kings and the Ahoms are examples of rulers who rose from such backgrounds.

slides.heading: Who were the zamindars?
slides.body_md: A **landed class** that did not cultivate, but held **milkiyat** and collected revenue.

rows: A landed class that did not cultivate directly
By caste and by services to the state
Personal property: could sell, bequeath or mortgage
By conquest or by colonising new land

visual.alt: Table, Zamindars. Who: A landed class that did not cultivate directly; Privileges: By caste and by services to the state; Milkiyat: Personal property: could sell, bequeath or mortgage; Duty: Collected revenue for the state; Rise: By conquest or by colonising new land
visual.caption: Zamindars

slides.narration: Zamindars were a landed class who did not cultivate directly but enjoyed social and economic privileges by virtue of their caste and their services to the state. They held milkiyat lands as personal property, which they could sell, bequeath or mortgage, and they collected revenue on behalf of the state. Many rose by conquest or by colonising new land.

slides.heading: Quick check: milkiyat
slides.body_md: Lands that zamindars held as personal property, which they could sell, bequeath or mortgage, were called ___.
slides.narration: Recall the term for personal property.

slides.heading: The armed strength of the zamindars

visual.alt: Table, Armed forces of the zamindars. Cavalry: 384,558; Infantry: 4,277,057; Elephants: 1,863; Cannon: 4,260; Boats: 4,500
visual.caption: Armed forces of the zamindars

slides.narration: Zamindars had fortresses called qilachas and armed contingents of cavalry, artillery and infantry. The Ain gives their forces as three hundred eighty four thousand cavalry, over four million infantry, eighteen hundred sixty three elephants, four thousand two hundred sixty cannon and four thousand five hundred boats. These figures show how important they were to the empire.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: patronage and exploitation
slides.body_md: Imagined zamindar of the lake villages: *digs a well, lends grain, demands extra labour at harvest.*

The mixture explains why peasants could both resent a zamindar and follow him in a revolt. Always ask whose account tells us this.

slides.heading: Land revenue: the terms
slides.body_md: **Jama** is assessed, **hasil** is collected; the **amil-guzar** collects.

visual.alt: Table, Revenue terms. Jama: The amount assessed; Hasil: The amount actually collected; Amil-guzar: The revenue collector; Zabt: Measurement of land under Akbar; Todar Mal: Akbar's revenue minister
visual.caption: Revenue terms

slides.narration: Land revenue was the economic mainstay of the empire, with revenue offices at different levels. Jama was the amount assessed, and hasil was the amount actually collected. The amil guzar was the revenue collector. Under Akbar, whose revenue minister was Todar Mal, the state tried to assess both cultivable and cultivated land by measurement, called zabt.

slides.narration: Land was classified by how often it was cultivated. Polaj was cultivated every year and never left fallow. Parauti was left fallow for a time to recover its strength. slides.heading: From measurement to payment
slides.body_md: Revenue was a **share of the crop**, paid in **cash or kind**.

nodes.label: Fix a share of the crop

visual.alt: Flow chart, Steps of assessment: Measure the land (zabt), then Class the land, then Fix a share of the crop, then Collect in cash or kind
visual.caption: Steps of assessment

slides.narration: The steps were these. First the land was measured, then it was classed, then a share of the crop was fixed as revenue, and finally the revenue was collected, in cash or in kind. This was the system of assessment that the state tried to apply across the empire, though results differed from year to year and place to place.

slides.heading: Mansabdars and jagirs
slides.body_md: A **mansab** was a rank with **zat** and **sawar**; many were paid by **jagirs**.

rows: A rank held in imperial service
A revenue assignment given in payment

visual.alt: Table, Mansabdars. Mansab: A rank held in imperial service; Zat: Personal rank and salary; Sawar: Number of horsemen to maintain; Jagir: A revenue assignment given in payment
visual.caption: Mansabdars

slides.narration: The mansabdari system linked rank with revenue. A mansabdar held a mansab, a rank. His zat was his personal rank and salary, and his sawar was the number of horsemen he had to maintain. Many mansabdars were paid not in cash from the treasury but by revenue assignments called jagirs.

slides.heading: The flow of silver
slides.body_md: Trade with the Americas and Europe brought **silver bullion** into India.

nodes.label: Indian textiles and spices in demand

visual.caption: The flow of silver

slides.narration: In the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, voyages of exploration and the opening of the Americas expanded world trade. India goods, such as textiles and spices, were in demand, and silver bullion flowed into India to pay for them. This helped the Mughal state to collect its revenue in cash.

notes.title: Peasants, Zamindars and the State — Notes

sections.heading: 1. Peasants and their holdings
sections.body_md:
In the Mughal countryside most people farmed. A peasant was a **raiyat** (plural riaya) or **muzarian**, or a **kisan** or **asami**. **Khud-kashta** cultivators lived in the village where they held land; **pahi-kashta** cultivators farmed in a village where they did not live, often for better terms or after moving.

**Land was plentiful and labour scarce**, which made movement common. An average peasant of north India seldom had more than a pair of bullocks and two ploughs; in Gujarat, a peasant with about six acres was counted as well off.

A non-resident cultivator who farmed land elsewhere.

sections.heading: 2. Water, seasons and crops
sections.body_md:
Farming depended on the **monsoon**, with irrigation from **wells, tanks and canals**; the **Persian wheel** was used in some regions. The state sometimes built or repaired canals, such as the **Shah Nahr** in the Punjab under Shah Jahan.

There were two seasons, **kharif** (autumn) and **rabi** (spring). The Ain says that Agra produced 39 kinds of crop and Delhi 43 over the two seasons, and Bengal had 50 varieties of rice alone. **Jins-i kamil**, literally perfect crops, were cash crops such as **cotton** and **sugarcane**, and also oilseeds and lentils. Crops from the Americas, by way of Africa and Spain, included **maize**, tomatoes, potatoes and chillies, pineapple and papaya.

sections.heading: 3. Sources: the Ain-i Akbari
sections.body_md:
The **Ain-i Akbari** was written by **Abu'l Fazl**, Akbar's court historian, and completed in **1598** after five revisions. It is the third part of the Akbarnama. Its aim was to present Akbar's empire as having a ruling class that ensured social harmony. It records arrangements for the imperial household, the army and revenue, and statistics of provinces.

It has **five books**: the first three describe the administration (**manzil-abadi**, the imperial household; **sipah-abadi**, military and civil administration; **mulk-abadi**, the fiscal side, with revenue rates and the **Account of the Twelve Provinces**); the fourth and fifth deal with religious, literary and cultural traditions and a collection of Akbar's auspicious sayings.

**Limits:** errors in totalling; data not collected evenly (the caste of zamindars is missing for some provinces, fiscal data for others); prices and wages largely from Agra and its surroundings. Even so it is extraordinarily valuable. Other sources: revenue records of Gujarat, Maharashtra and Rajasthan (17th and 18th centuries), East India Company records and petitions.

sections.heading: 4. The village community and women
sections.body_md:
The village had three constituents: **cultivators, the panchayat and the headman** (**muqaddam** or **mandal**). The headman was chosen by consensus, approved by the zamindar, and kept accounts with the **patwari**. The **panchayat**, an assembly of elders and usually heads of families, had representatives of different castes in mixed villages but was dominated by the powerful. It had a common fund, kept caste boundaries and could impose fines and expulsion. Caste (jati) panchayats in Rajasthan arbitrated disputes, and petitions show lower castes complaining of heavy tax demands or forced labour by upper castes and officials.

**Caste inequality** was deep: menial labourers lived on the margins, among Muslim communities the halalkhoran were housed outside the village, and in Bihar the mallahzadas are recorded as comparable to slaves. **Artisans** (potters, blacksmiths, carpenters, barbers, goldsmiths) were paid with a share of the harvest, a plot, or both; in Maharashtra such land was **miras** or **watan**. British officials called villages **little republics**, but there was no social equality and historians question the term.

**Women** worked alongside men in sowing, weeding, threshing and winnowing, and in spinning, sieving, clay work and embroidery. As their labour was valued, **bride-price** was common among peasants and artisans, and remarriage of divorced and widowed women was legitimate. Men controlled the household; women petitioned panchayats; women of the landed gentry could inherit property, and the Rajshahi zamindari in eighteenth-century Bengal was held by a woman.

sections.heading: 5. Forests and tribes; zamindars
sections.body_md:
Forest dwellers were called **jangli**, which in Mughal usage meant people whose livelihood came from forest produce, hunting and shifting cultivation, not "savage". The state needed elephants and asked forest peoples to supply them as **peshkash**, a form of tribute. Court writers described hunts (**shikar**) as occasions to dispense justice. Honey, beeswax and gum lac went to distant markets; the Koch kings and the Ahoms of Assam, and forest chiefs who became zamindars or kings, show change through trade, state demands and social factors.

**Zamindars** were a landed class that did not directly cultivate but had social and economic privileges by caste and services to the state. They held **milkiyat** lands as personal property, collected revenue for the state, and kept **qilachas** (fortresses) and armed contingents. The Ain gives their forces as 384,558 cavalry, 4,277,057 infantry, 1,863 elephants, 4,260 cannon and 4,500 boats. Many had come to their position by conquest or by colonising new land. Their relation with peasants combined **exploitation and patronage**, and many peasant revolts were led by zamindars with peasant support.

sections.heading: 6. Land revenue and the mansabdars
sections.body_md:
Land revenue was the **economic mainstay** of the empire, with offices at different levels. **Jama** was the amount assessed and **hasil** the amount actually collected; the **amil-guzar** was the collector. Under Akbar, with **Todar Mal** as revenue minister, the state tried to assess cultivable and cultivated land through measurement (**zabt**). Land was classed as **polaj** (cultivated every year), **parauti** (fallow for a time to recover), **chachar** (fallow three or four years) and **banjar** (uncultivated five years or more). Revenue was fixed as a share of the crop and paid in cash or kind.

In the **mansabdari system**, a mansabdar held a rank (**mansab**) with **zat** (personal rank and salary) and **sawar** (the number of horsemen to maintain). Many were paid by revenue assignments called **jagirs**.

key_terms.definition_md: The revenue assessed, and the revenue actually collected.

sections.heading: 7. The flow of silver
sections.body_md:
In the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, voyages of exploration and the opening of the Americas expanded world trade. India's goods, especially textiles and spices, were in demand abroad, and **silver bullion** flowed into India to pay for them. This helped the Mughal state to **collect revenue in cash**.

The Italian traveller **Giovanni Careri**, who passed through India about 1690, described silver from all over the world coming to India. A traveller's remark is useful evidence of how a visitor saw the trade, but it is not a count of coin: historians check it against mint and trade records, and weigh other causes of cash revenue such as more land under cultivation and higher prices.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Calling the Ain-i Akbari a neutral record; it presents an official view and its data are uneven.
- Treating all peasants alike; name khud-kashta and pahi-kashta.
- Writing that Mughal villages were equal; historians question the little republic view.
- Mixing up jama (assessed) and hasil (collected).
- Writing jangli as savage; it described a way of living.
- Calling zamindars cultivators; they held milkiyat and collected revenue.
- Giving silver as the only cause of cash revenue.
- Quoting a figure without saying what it cannot show.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1 mark: one correct option.
- 2 marks: two points, or a point and a reason (30–50 words).
- 3 marks: three distinct points (50–80 words).
- 5 marks: five headed points (80–120 words); assess questions need more than one side and a judgement.

questions.stem_md: Which pair of terms was commonly used in Mughal-period sources for a peasant?

options.text_md: Zamindar or jagirdar
Raiyat (plural riaya) or muzarian
Muqaddam or patwari
Mansabdar or sawar

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Raiyat (plural riaya) or muzarian. The other pairs name landholders, village officials and ranks in the imperial service, not cultivators.

questions.stem_md: Meera's family lives in village X and cultivates fields in X and also in village Y, where the revenue terms are lighter. Ghulam moved from X to Y two years ago and cultivates only in Y, where he now lives. Which description uses the Mughal-period terms correctly?

options.text_md: Meera is pahi-kashta in both villages; Ghulam is pahi-kashta in Y
Meera is khud-kashta in both villages; Ghulam is pahi-kashta in Y
Meera is pahi-kashta in X and khud-kashta in Y; Ghulam is khud-kashta in X
Meera is khud-kashta in X and pahi-kashta in Y; Ghulam is khud-kashta in Y

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Meera is khud-kashta in X and pahi-kashta in Y; Ghulam is khud-kashta in Y. Apply the test of residence to each village separately: living in the village where the land lies makes a cultivator khud-kashta there, and cultivating land in a village where one does not live makes him pahi-kashta there.

questions.stem_md: Historians connect the movement of peasants between villages with the fact that land was plentiful and labour scarce. Which finding about an imagined province would most weaken this connection?

options.text_md: Records showing that land was scarce and labour plentiful there, yet peasants moved between villages as often as elsewhere
A record of peasants moving to a village that offered easier terms
Records of new villages founded on uncleared land
A petition from a village asking that cultivators who had left be called back

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Records showing that land was scarce and labour plentiful there, yet peasants moved between villages as often as elsewhere. To weaken a link between a cause and an effect, the effect must appear without the cause. The other findings are the kind of movement that plentiful land and scarce labour would produce.

questions.stem_md: Which of these crops reached India after the opening of the Americas, travelling by way of Africa and Spain?

options.text_md: Sugarcane
Wheat
Maize
Lentils

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Maize. Maize was among the new crops from the Americas. The other three were already part of farming in the subcontinent.

questions.stem_md: An imagined, undated household account from a village lists chillies and tomatoes among the foods bought at a fair, along with rice and lentils. Which dating judgement is soundest?

options.text_md: It was written before 1492, since rice and lentils were already old crops in India
It cannot be dated at all, since the list names no ruler and no year
It was written after the Americas were opened to world trade, since chillies and tomatoes came from there, but the list alone does not show how long after
It was written in Akbar's reign, since chillies were brought to India by his officials

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** It was written after the Americas were opened to world trade, since chillies and tomatoes came from there, but the list alone does not show how long after. A single late item in a list sets an earliest possible date for the whole list, while older items such as rice set no limit at all. Nothing in the list ties it to one ruler.

questions.stem_md: What did the term jins-i kamil, literally perfect crops, refer to?

options.text_md: Cash crops such as cotton and sugarcane
Crops grown only for the cultivator's own meals
Crops that the state did not tax
Crops grown only in forest clearings

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Cash crops such as cotton and sugarcane. The word marks crops grown largely for sale. Oilseeds and lentils could also be counted here.

questions.stem_md: An imagined register shows that a village paid its revenue in cash and that most of its fields were under cotton and sugarcane, sold at a weekly market. Which inference is the most careful?

options.text_md: Its peasants grew nothing for their own food
The state had forbidden the growing of food crops there
The village was held by a zamindar who owned all its produce
Its peasants were closely linked to markets, but the register cannot show whether they gained or lost by this

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Its peasants were closely linked to markets, but the register cannot show whether they gained or lost by this. The register supports a claim about market links. Claims about food supply, orders from the state or ownership go beyond what it records, and nothing in it shows who benefited.

questions.stem_md: The Ain-i Akbari was written by ___, the court historian of Akbar, and was completed in ___.
questions.solution_md: Abu'l Fazl completed the work in 1598.

questions.stem_md: True or false? The Ain-i Akbari gives the same kinds of data, equally complete, for every province of the empire.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **False.** Data were not gathered evenly: some provinces lack information that others have, so comparisons across provinces need care.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Historians read the Ain-i Akbari as an official view of the empire and not as a neutral record.

**Reason (R):** Its author was Akbar's court historian, and his aim was to present the empire as one whose ruling class secured social harmony.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** The author's post and purpose are what make the work an official picture.

questions.stem_md: Name the two cropping seasons of Mughal agriculture and explain what the term jins-i kamil meant.
questions.solution_md: Two seasons named, and the meaning of the term with examples.

answer.model_answer_md: The two seasons were **kharif** (autumn) and **rabi** (spring), so many fields could yield two harvests in a year. **Jins-i kamil**, literally perfect crops, meant cash crops such as **cotton** and **sugarcane**, grown for sale; oilseeds and lentils also came under it.

questions.stem_md: A student wants to write about the wages of labourers in a village of Bengal and plans to rely only on the wage tables of the Ain-i Akbari. Is this wise? Give one point in favour and one against.
questions.solution_md: One strength of the source and the limit set by where its data came from.

answer.model_answer_md: **For:** the Ain is an extraordinarily rich official record, with prices and wages that historians value. **Against:** its prices and wages come largely from Agra and its surroundings, so they may not fit a Bengal village; she should add local records.

questions.stem_md: An imagined register gives, for three villages, the area under jins-i kamil and the total cultivated area (in bighas): Village A, 40 of 200; Village B, 90 of 180; Village C, 10 of 150. questions.solution_md: Three shares computed, the village identified and the limit of area figures stated.

answer.model_answer_md: **Shares:** A, 40 of 200 is 20 per cent; B, 90 of 180 is 50 per cent; C, 10 of 150 is about 7 per cent. **Village B** was the most tied to the market, since half its land grew crops meant for sale. **Limit:** area alone does not show how much was sold, at what price, or whether the peasants gained.

marking_scheme.step: Village B named with a reason

questions.stem_md: Describe the peasants and agricultural production of the Mughal countryside in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries.
questions.solution_md: Peasant types, holdings and mobility, water, seasons and cash crops, and the new crops.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Peasants:** called raiyat or muzarian, or kisan and asami; khud-kashta lived in the village of their land, pahi-kashta cultivated elsewhere, often after moving to better terms.
2. **Holdings:** in north India an average peasant seldom had more than a pair of bullocks and two ploughs; in Gujarat about six acres meant comfort. Land was plentiful and labour scarce.
3. **Water:** agriculture depended on the monsoon, helped by wells, tanks and canals, with the Persian wheel in places.
4. **Crops:** kharif and rabi harvests; cash crops (jins-i kamil) such as cotton and sugarcane.
5. **New crops:** maize, tomatoes, potatoes, chillies, pineapple and papaya came from the Americas.

questions.stem_md: An imagined historian wants to describe how well off the peasants of a Gujarat village were around 1650. She has the Ain-i Akbari (completed in 1598), revenue records of Gujarat from the seventeenth century, and an imagined petition from the village. Assess how she should use each source and how firm her conclusion can be.
questions.solution_md: The Ain, local records and the petition weighed in turn, then a method and a measured conclusion.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **The Ain** gives an official, provincial picture, written for the emperor's court and half a century earlier, so it suits a broad background but not this village.
2. **Gujarat revenue records** are closer in place and time and show what was demanded, but the state made them for its own purposes.
3. **The petition** gives the villagers' side and their grievances, yet it is one document and may not be typical.
4. **Method:** she should set the three side by side, using the benchmark that about six acres was comfortable in Gujarat, and see where they agree.
5. **Judgement:** her conclusion must be cautious, a likely range, not a firm account of every household.

questions.stem_md: Read the source, a SOYL summary of what a kind of work contains, and answer the questions that follow. *(Summary written by SOYL in its own words for practice; it is not a quotation or translation of any source.)*
questions.solution_md:
**(a)** It is the part of Abu'l Fazl's history of the reign that describes the empire's arrangements.

**(b)** Link the place the data came from to how far they can be generalised.

**(c) (i)** A local record of the right period and what it can check.

**OR (c) (ii)** Two questions on coverage and on accuracy and purpose.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** The **Ain-i Akbari**, the third part of the Akbarnama.

**(b)** They may not represent **other regions**, so conclusions about distant places need other records.

**OR (c) (ii)** (1) **Were the data collected evenly** for every province, or are some details missing for this one? (2) **Are the totals correct**, since errors in adding figures are known, and who gathered the data for what purpose?

questions.passage_md:
**What a great court history of Akbar's reign contains (summary)**

A court historian of Akbar finished a large work near the end of the sixteenth century, as the last part of a longer history of the reign. Its first books describe how the empire was run: the emperor's household, the army and the nobles and servants of the state, and the fiscal side, with the rates of revenue and, for each province, tables on matters such as its revenue, its zamindars and their forces. Its later books turn to the beliefs and traditions of the people and to sayings of the emperor. The tables of prices and wages come mostly from Agra and the lands around it.

answer.model_answer_md: They may not represent **other regions**, so conclusions about distant places need other records.

questions.stem_md: Which three constituents are named for the village community in accounts of the Mughal countryside?

options.text_md: Zamindars, mansabdars and the revenue collector
Cultivators, the panchayat and the village headman
Priests, merchants and artisans
The patwari, the jagirdar and the emperor

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Cultivators, the panchayat and the village headman. The village community was made up of those who farmed, the elders' assembly and the headman. The other groups were outside it or are only part of it.

questions.stem_md: Some historians question the nineteenth-century British description of Mughal villages as little republics. Which finding about an imagined village would most strengthen their doubt?

options.text_md: Panchayat records showing that fines and expulsions were decided by heads of dominant families, with lower-caste households having no voice
Records of a common fund that paid for mending the village well
A headman chosen after discussion among the cultivators
Cultivators of several castes living in one village

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Panchayat records showing that fines and expulsions were decided by heads of dominant families, with lower-caste households having no voice. The doubt concerns equality. Only the first finding shows power being held unequally; a shared fund, a chosen headman and mixed castes can all be found in a village with deep divisions.

questions.stem_md: Why was bride-price, rather than dowry, common in peasant and artisan communities?

options.text_md: Women were forbidden to work outside the home, so the groom's family paid for their upkeep
Women's labour in fields and workshops was valued, so the bride's family was compensated
The state fixed the amount that a groom had to pay
Remarriage was banned, so the first marriage had to be costly

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Women's labour in fields and workshops was valued, so the bride's family was compensated. The custom is linked with the economic worth of women's work. The other options contradict the evidence on women's work or on remarriage.

questions.stem_md: Historians link bride-price with the value of women's work in peasant and artisan households. Which finding about imagined communities would most weaken that link?

options.text_md: Communities in which women spun, sieved and worked clay paid bride-price
A woman petitioning a panchayat against a husband who neglected her
Communities in which women did no field or craft work paid bride-price just as often
Divorced and widowed women remarrying in a community

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Communities in which women did no field or craft work paid bride-price just as often. A causal link is weakened when the effect is found where the supposed cause is absent. The other findings do not separate bride-price from women's work.

questions.stem_md: In Mughal agrarian society, among which group did women have the right to inherit property?

options.text_md: Landless labourers
Village artisans
Forest-dwelling hunters
The landed gentry

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** The landed gentry. The right is recorded for women of the landed gentry. In the eighteenth century a zamindari in Bengal, Rajshahi, was held by a woman.

questions.stem_md: A historian wants to know what grievances villagers, women among them, took to the panchayat. Which source would serve her best?

options.text_md: The revenue tables for each province in the Ain-i Akbari
A chronicle of the emperor's campaigns
A list of mansabdars and their ranks
Surviving petitions addressed to panchayats

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Surviving petitions addressed to panchayats. Match the source to the question: only petitions were made by villagers to the panchayat. The others record provinces, wars and ranks.

questions.stem_md: Match each term with the correct description.

options.text_md: Muqaddam or mandal
Patwari
Pahi-kashta
Miras or watan

match_right.text_md: The village accountant who helped the headman keep accounts
Land given to a village artisan in parts of Maharashtra
A cultivator who cultivated land in a village other than his own

questions.solution_md: **Key:** (a)–(r), (b)–(p), (c)–(s), (d)–(q). Each term is the usual name for the role described.

questions.stem_md: True or false? Because nineteenth-century British officials called Mughal villages little republics, historians today accept that villagers enjoyed social equality.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **False.** Historians question the term, since caste-based inequalities ran deep and the powerful dominated the panchayat.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Petitions from lower-caste cultivators to panchayats show that panchayats treated every caste alike.

**Reason (R):** In villages of mixed castes the panchayat had representatives of different castes, though the powerful dominated it.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** The petitions record complaints, which is not the same as fair treatment; the second claim is correct and itself points to domination.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Women of peasant households worked in sowing, weeding, threshing and winnowing.

**Reason (R):** Men controlled the household in agrarian society.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Both are accurate, but male control of the household does not account for women's field work, which arose from the needs of cultivation.

questions.stem_md: An imagined panchayat fines a household for crossing a caste boundary. Name the two powers that the panchayat was using, and one question a historian should ask about who made the decision.
questions.solution_md: Two powers recognised and a question about who held power in the panchayat.

answer.model_answer_md: The panchayat was using its power to **keep caste boundaries** and to **impose fines**; it could also order expulsion. A historian should ask **who sat on it**, since the powerful dominated panchayats, and whether the fined household had any voice.

questions.stem_md: An imagined panchayat record says that a woman complained that her husband neglected her and asked the elders to act. State one conclusion about women in village society and one limit of a single record.
questions.solution_md: A conclusion about women's recourse and a limit set by one record.

answer.model_answer_md: **Conclusion:** women were not without a voice, since they could bring complaints about their households before the panchayat and seek a hearing. **Limit:** one record cannot show how the elders decided, how often women did this, or whether women of every caste could.

questions.stem_md: A historian finds that in an imagined village most artisan families, such as potters and blacksmiths, were paid a share of each harvest, while one carpenter family held a plot of land as well. Suggest three explanations for this difference.
questions.solution_md: Three possible reasons from the nature of the work, custom and resources, with a caution.

answer.model_answer_md: (1) The carpenter's work may have been needed all year, so the village gave a **plot** as a lasting reward. (2) The family may have held the plot under an **earlier arrangement** that custom or a village agreement kept alive. (3) The village may have had **land to spare** when grain was short. One record cannot decide between these.

questions.stem_md: An imagined village's records show that its panchayat kept a common fund from household contributions and used it to repair the village well; that the headman was chosen after discussion and approved by the zamindar; and that elders from dominant families fined a lower-caste household for breaking a caste boundary. Using this and what you know, assess the view that Mughal villages were little republics.
questions.solution_md: Evidence for self-government, evidence against, inequality, other records and a balanced verdict.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **For the view:** a common fund paid for a shared need, and the headman was chosen by consensus, so villagers did manage some affairs themselves.
2. **Against:** the headman needed the zamindar's approval, so the village was not wholly self-governing.
3. **Inequality:** the elders came from dominant families and fined a lower-caste household, which shows power held unequally.
4. **Wider evidence:** petitions from lower castes complain of heavy demands and forced labour.
5. **Judgement:** the description fits the village's self-management but hides caste divisions, which is why historians question it.

questions.stem_md: Read the source, an imagined petition summary, and answer the questions that follow. *(Imagined document written by SOYL for practice; the people in it are not real, though the evidence and events in the background are.)*
questions.solution_md:
**(a)** The headman kept accounts with the help of this official.

**(b)** Read the choice of audience as a sign of what the petitioners expected.

**(c) (i)** Two limits of a single, one-sided document.

**OR (c) (ii)** Two kinds of record that can check the claim.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** The **patwari**, or village accountant.

**(b)** They saw it as a body that could **hear complaints and press an official**, a place to seek justice.

**OR (c) (ii)** (1) **Revenue records of the village**, which would show the rate of demand actually entered. (2) **Other petitions or the elders' reply**, which would show whether the same complaint was made elsewhere or was upheld.

questions.stem_md: In Mughal usage, the term jangli was applied to people whose living came mainly from

options.text_md: serving as cavalry in the imperial army
trading cloth in distant ports
gathering forest produce, hunting and shifting cultivation
holding the right to collect revenue from villages

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** gathering forest produce, hunting and shifting cultivation. The word described a way of living, not a judgement that such people were savage.

questions.stem_md: An imagined official's note describes two communities living in the same forest. Community P gathers honey and beeswax, hunts, and clears a patch of forest every few years to sow a crop before moving on. Community Q lives in a clearing, ploughs the same fields every year and sells grain in a nearby town. Which community would a Mughal official have called jangli, and why?

options.text_md: Q, because it lives inside the forest
P, because its living comes from forest produce, hunting and shifting cultivation
Both, because both live among trees
Neither, because jangli was a word for zamindars

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** P, because its living comes from forest produce, hunting and shifting cultivation. The label rested on how a community made its living, not on where it lived. Test each community against that criterion; the one that farms fixed fields and sells grain does not meet it.

questions.stem_md: An imagined record says that a forest chief sent elephants to a Mughal officer every year and was left in control of his forest lands. Which inference is the most careful?

options.text_md: The tribute was part of a working relationship between the chief and the state, but the record alone cannot show whether he gave it willingly
The chief was a salaried officer of the empire
The state had no interest in forest lands
The chief had been conquered and his lands taken away

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** The tribute was part of a working relationship between the chief and the state, but the record alone cannot show whether he gave it willingly. The record links the gift and the chief's continued control, which supports a claim about a relationship. Rank in the empire, indifference of the state and conquest are not stated, and willingness cannot be read from it.

questions.stem_md: Court chroniclers described imperial hunts (shikar) as occasions on which the emperor dispensed justice. For which question would such a chronicle be the weakest evidence?

options.text_md: How the court wished the hunts to be seen
How the forest peoples themselves experienced the hunts
Which hunts took place in which years, as the court recorded them
What ceremony surrounded an imperial hunt

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** How the forest peoples themselves experienced the hunts. A chronicle is written from the court's side. It is useful for the court's own view and ceremonies, and weakest where the people it does not speak for are concerned.

questions.stem_md: Which finding would best support the view that trade in forest produce could change the position of a forest chief?

options.text_md: A record of a chief sending elephants as tribute to a Mughal officer
A chronicle's account of an emperor's hunt in a forest
A list of the crops grown by plains peasants
Records of a chief who supplied honey and gum lac to a market town and later appears as a revenue-paying zamindar with armed followers

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Records of a chief who supplied honey and gum lac to a market town and later appears as a revenue-paying zamindar with armed followers. The claim needs a chain from trade to a changed position. Tribute and hunting concern the state, and plains crops concern a different group.

questions.stem_md: Historians describe the relation of zamindars and peasants as one of both exploitation and patronage. Which finding would most weaken the claim that zamindars could act as patrons?

options.text_md: Records of many zamindars showing no gift, loan, tank or well for tenants, only demands for extra payment and labour
A zamindar who sheltered his tenants in a famine
A zamindar who had a tank dug for a village
A revolt led by a zamindar with peasant support

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Records of many zamindars showing no gift, loan, tank or well for tenants, only demands for extra payment and labour. The other findings are acts of patronage or support from peasants. Only a pattern of no benefits at all would count against the claim.

questions.stem_md: The Ain-i Akbari gives the armed forces of the zamindars as 384,558 cavalry and 4,277,057 infantry, besides elephants, cannon and boats. Roughly how many foot soldiers were there for each horseman, and what does it suggest?

options.text_md: About 3, so cavalry formed the main part
About 25, so cavalry was a tiny fraction
About 11, so zamindar forces were mainly infantry
About 1, so the two were equal

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** About 11, so zamindar forces were mainly infantry. Divide 4,277,057 by 384,558, which gives a little over 11. The other ratios do not match the figures.

questions.stem_md: Lands that zamindars held as personal property, which they could sell, bequeath or mortgage, were called ___.
questions.solution_md: Such lands were milkiyat.

questions.stem_md: True or false? Zamindars were a landed class who mainly cultivated their fields with their own labour.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **False.** They did not directly cultivate; they enjoyed privileges through caste and services to the state, and others worked their lands.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Many zamindars owed their position to conquest or to colonising new land.

**Reason (R):** Zamindars enjoyed social privileges by virtue of their caste.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Both are true, but caste privilege does not explain how a family came to hold land through conquest or settlement.

**Assertion (A):** Forest produce such as honey, beeswax and gum lac reached distant markets.

**Reason (R):** The Mughal state placed no demands on forest peoples and had no dealings with them.

Choose the correct option.

Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** The trade is recorded; the second claim is false, since the state asked for elephants as tribute and dealt with forest chiefs.

questions.stem_md: Name two ways in which the state and trade affected forest peoples in the Mughal period.
questions.solution_md: One effect from the state and one from trade.

answer.model_answer_md: The state asked forest peoples for **elephants as peshkash**, a form of tribute. **Trade in forest produce** such as honey, beeswax and gum lac with distant markets also changed their lives, and some chiefs became zamindars or kings.

questions.stem_md: An imagined zamindar sells part of his milkiyat land to a merchant. He still collects the revenue of his villages for the state. What two things does this suggest about the nature of a zamindar's rights?
questions.solution_md: Property that can be sold, set beside a duty to the state that continues.

answer.model_answer_md: **Milkiyat** was personal property, so it could be sold like any holding. His role in **collecting revenue for the state** was a separate right or service, not the same as owning every field in his villages.

marking_scheme.step: Revenue role as a separate right or service

questions.stem_md: An imagined note says a zamindar lent seed to his tenants in a bad year but also made them work on his fort without wages. Explain what this shows about zamindars and peasants, and why many peasant revolts could still be led by zamindars.
questions.solution_md: The two sides of the relation and the reason a revolt could unite both.

answer.model_answer_md: The note shows **two sides** of the relation: **patronage** (seed in a bad year) and **exploitation** (unpaid labour). Because a zamindar could be both protector and oppressor, peasants might follow him when he defied the state, and many zamindar-led revolts had **peasant support**, even if the same tenants resented his demands in other years.

marking_scheme.step: Why peasants could still support a zamindar-led revolt

questions.stem_md: Describe the position, powers and role of zamindars in the Mughal countryside.
questions.solution_md: Position, property, revenue role, armed strength and the origin and peasant relations.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Position:** a landed class that did not cultivate directly but had social and economic privileges by caste and service to the state.
2. **Property:** they held milkiyat lands that they could sell, bequeath or mortgage.
3. **Revenue:** they collected revenue on behalf of the state.
4. **Force:** they kept forts and armed contingents; the Ain records over four million infantry and about 384,000 cavalry for the zamindars as a whole.
5. **Rise and peasants:** many rose by conquest or colonising new land; their relation with peasants combined exploitation and patronage, and many revolts were zamindar-led with peasant support.

questions.stem_md: Read the source, an imagined revenue official's note, and answer the questions that follow. *(Imagined document written by SOYL for practice; the people in it are not real, though the evidence and events in the background are.)*
questions.solution_md:
**(a)** Such lands could be sold, bequeathed or mortgaged.

**(b)** Look for an act of help that could win loyalty.

**(c) (i)** Two kinds of evidence from outside the two accounts.

**(b)** He **opened his grain stores** in the dry months, so villagers saw him as a source of help.

questions.stem_md: In the Mughal land revenue system, what was the difference between jama and hasil?

options.text_md: Jama was the amount paid in cash and hasil the amount paid in kind
Jama was revenue from cultivated land and hasil from forest land
Jama was the amount assessed and hasil the amount actually collected
Jama was the share of the zamindar and hasil the share of the state

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Jama was the amount assessed and hasil the amount actually collected. One word names the assessment and the other the collection, so the two could differ in any year.

questions.stem_md: An imagined village accountant's register lists the village's land in four classes: polaj, 120 bighas; parauti, 60 bighas; chachar, 45 bighas; and banjar, 75 bighas. Which statement follows from the register?

options.text_md: Polaj, cultivated every year, was 40 per cent of the whole, and chachar was 15 per cent
Polaj was 20 per cent of the whole and parauti was 40 per cent
Banjar was 15 per cent of the whole and chachar was 25 per cent
Land cultivated every year or left fallow for a time to recover made up only 40 per cent

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Polaj, cultivated every year, was 40 per cent of the whole, and chachar was 15 per cent. The total is 300 bighas. Polaj is 120 of 300, which is 40 per cent, and chachar is 45 of 300, which is 15 per cent. Polaj and parauti together make 180 of 300, which is 60 per cent.

questions.stem_md: An imagined district's records give jama and hasil in thousands of rupees. Year 1: jama 200, hasil 190. Year 2: jama 200, hasil 120. Year 3: jama 210, hasil 189. Which inference is the most careful?

options.text_md: Year 3 had the largest shortfall because its jama was the highest
Year 2 proves that the peasants of the district were in revolt
Year 1 shows that the assessment was too low
Year 2 had the largest gap, 40 per cent of the jama, but the records do not say whether failed rains, flight of peasants or lax collection caused it

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Year 2 had the largest gap, 40 per cent of the jama, but the records do not say whether failed rains, flight of peasants or lax collection caused it. The gaps are 10, 80 and 21, which are 5, 40 and 10 per cent of the jama. The figures show how large the gaps were; they do not show why.

questions.stem_md: Two imagined mansabdars have these ranks. Karan: zat 1,000 and sawar 400. Imran: zat 800 and sawar 600. Which statement is correct?

options.text_md: Imran has the higher personal rank and must also maintain more horsemen
Karan has the higher personal rank and salary rank, while Imran must maintain more horsemen
Karan has the higher personal rank and must also maintain more horsemen
They have the same personal rank, but Karan must maintain more horsemen

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Karan has the higher personal rank and salary rank, while Imran must maintain more horsemen. Zat is personal rank and salary, and sawar is the number of horsemen to maintain; compare each number with the right meaning.

questions.stem_md: Historians argue that the inflow of silver helped the Mughal state to collect revenue in cash. Which finding about an imagined province would most weaken this view for that province?

options.text_md: Records showing that in years when much silver reached its ports, its revenue was still paid almost entirely in kind
Records showing its mints striking more coins in such years
Records showing that its revenue demands were fixed in cash
Records of merchants paying silver for textiles at its ports

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Records showing that in years when much silver reached its ports, its revenue was still paid almost entirely in kind. The claim links silver to cash collection. Evidence that silver arrived with no change in how revenue was paid breaks the link; the other findings fit it.

questions.stem_md: A historian has a traveller's remark that silver from all over the world came to India, the ledger of a mint, and a revenue register. For which question is the mint ledger the most useful evidence?

options.text_md: How a foreign visitor explained the flow of silver
How many coins were struck in particular years, which can be set beside accounts of silver arriving
How much revenue a village was assessed to pay
What the emperor thought about foreign trade

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** How many coins were struck in particular years, which can be set beside accounts of silver arriving. A mint ledger records production of coin. A visitor's explanation, village assessments and the emperor's views are better found in other documents.

questions.stem_md: An imagined province shows a steep rise in the revenue collected in cash between 1580 and 1650. A historian suspects the inflow of silver but knows that more land under cultivation could also explain it. Which further evidence would best help her separate the two explanations?

options.text_md: A list of the crops that came from the Americas
A portrait of the governor of the province
Records of the area under cultivation and of coin struck in the province across the same years
A chronicle's praise of the emperor's generosity

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Records of the area under cultivation and of coin struck in the province across the same years. Competing explanations are told apart by data that bear on each: cultivated area for the one, coin supply for the other. The remaining items bear on neither.

questions.stem_md: Match each class of land with its description.

options.text_md: Polaj
Parauti
Chachar
Banjar

match_right.text_md: Left uncultivated for five years or more
Cultivated every year and never left fallow
Left fallow for three or four years
Left fallow for a time to recover its strength

questions.solution_md: **Key:** (a)–(q), (b)–(s), (c)–(r), (d)–(p). The classes run from constant use to long rest.

questions.stem_md: Arrange these events in chronological order, earliest first.

options.text_md: An Italian traveller passes through India
Abu'l Fazl completes the Ain-i Akbari
Shah Jahan's officers build the Shah Nahr canal in the Punjab
Voyages of exploration open the Americas to world trade

questions.solution_md: **Correct order:** (d) → (b) → (c) → (a). They fall in the years from 1492, in 1598, in Shah Jahan's reign (1628 to 1658) and about 1690.

marking_scheme.step: Complete correct sequence (all items in place)

questions.stem_md: Arrange these links in the order in which each led to the next.

options.text_md: The Mughal state finds it easier to collect revenue in cash
Silver bullion flows into India to pay for them
Foreign merchants seek Indian textiles and spices
Voyages of exploration open the Americas and expand world trade

questions.solution_md: **Correct order:** (d) → (c) → (b) → (a). Each step makes the next possible: trade creates demand, demand is paid for in silver, and silver supplies coin.

questions.stem_md: The official who collected land revenue for the Mughal state was called the ___.
questions.solution_md: The revenue collector was the amil-guzar.

questions.stem_md: True or false? In the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries silver bullion flowed into India in payment for goods such as textiles and spices.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **True.** Demand for Indian goods abroad was met largely with silver.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The jama recorded for a province shows what the treasury expected, not necessarily what it received.

**Reason (R):** Jama was the amount assessed, while hasil was the amount actually collected.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** The difference between the two terms is exactly why an assessed figure cannot stand for receipts.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Large silver imports at a port do not by themselves prove that cash revenue grew in the interior.

**Reason (R):** Silver that reaches a port may be spent, hoarded or made into ornaments before it reaches the revenue-paying villages or the treasury.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** The missing link between arrival and spread is the reason caution is needed, so R explains A.

questions.stem_md: Explain the terms jama and hasil, and say who the amil-guzar was.
questions.solution_md: The two terms and the collector's office.

answer.model_answer_md: **Jama** was the amount of revenue assessed; **hasil** was the amount actually collected. The **amil-guzar** was the revenue collector, the official who carried out the collection for the state.

questions.stem_md: How did silver come to flow into India in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, and how did this help the Mughal state?
questions.solution_md: The trade that brought silver and its use in revenue.

answer.model_answer_md: Voyages of exploration and the opening of the Americas widened world trade, and demand for Indian textiles and spices was met with **silver bullion** that came into India. This supplied the coin that helped the Mughal state to collect its revenue in **cash**.

marking_scheme.step: Help in collecting revenue in cash

questions.stem_md: An imagined register shows 60 bighas of polaj and 40 bighas of parauti, of which 10 are under crop this year. The assessment is 4 rupees for each bigha under crop. Find the jama, and the share of the cultivated land that is polaj.
questions.solution_md: Cropped area and jama, then the polaj share.

answer.model_answer_md: Land under crop is 60 + 10 = 70 bighas. **Jama = 70 × 4 = 280 rupees.** Polaj is 60 of these 70 bighas, about 86 per cent, because polaj is cultivated every year.

marking_scheme.step: Polaj share of about 86 per cent

questions.stem_md: An imagined revenue official finds that land a village register lists as banjar has been cleared and sown for two years in a row. Explain how its classification and the revenue demand on it should change, and why the state measured cultivable as well as cultivated land. Three points.
questions.solution_md: Reclassification, the effect on the demand and the purpose of measuring cultivable land.

answer.model_answer_md: (1) It no longer fits **banjar**, land uncultivated for five years or more, and would now count as cultivated land, **polaj** if it went on being sown every year. (2) Cropped land carried a revenue demand, so the **jama would rise**. (3) Measuring **cultivable** land let the state see land that could be brought under the plough and plan to extend cultivation and revenue.

questions.stem_md: An imagined province shows a steep rise in cash revenue between 1580 and 1650. Give three possible explanations other than a higher rate of assessment, and say what evidence could separate them.
questions.solution_md: Three rival explanations with the evidence that bears on each.

answer.model_answer_md: (1) **More silver** reached the province, so cash was easier to find. (2) **More land** came under cultivation, so there was more to assess. (3) **Prices rose**, so the same crop fetched more coin. Mint records, measurement records of cultivated area and price records for the same years could tell these apart.

questions.stem_md: Assess how far the Mughal land revenue system depended on the accurate measurement of land.
questions.solution_md: Measurement, classes, the jama-hasil gap, local intermediaries and a weighed verdict.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Foundation:** zabt under Akbar and Todar Mal fixed revenue on measured land.
2. **Classes:** the four land classes needed knowledge of cultivation over several years.
3. **Gap:** jama and hasil differed in practice because of weather, flight of peasants and local officials.
4. **Intermediaries:** zamindars, headmen and patwaris mediated measurement, so local power could shape the figures.
5. **Judgement:** measurement was the foundation of the system's claims, but collection depended as much on local intermediaries and harvests, so accuracy was only part of the story.

questions.stem_md: Assess how far the flow of silver explains the Mughal state's ability to collect land revenue in cash.
questions.solution_md: The flow, the link, the strength of the evidence, other factors and a balanced verdict.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **The flow:** exploration and the opening of the Americas expanded trade, and silver came into India to pay for textiles and spices.
2. **The link:** more bullion meant more coin, which made cash payment of revenue easier.
3. **Evidence:** an Italian traveller who passed through India about 1690 described silver from many lands reaching India, but a visitor's remark is not a count of coin.
4. **Other factors:** the machinery of measurement and assessment, and markets that let peasants sell crops for cash, also mattered.
5. **Judgement:** silver was an important condition but not the sole cause; the case is strongest when mint and revenue records agree.

questions.stem_md: Read the source, an imagined village accountant's register, and answer the questions that follow. *(Imagined document written by SOYL for practice; the people in it are not real, though the evidence and events in the background are.)*

questions.stem_md: An imagined, undated village register says that the fields were measured in the manner described in the Ain-i Akbari and refers to the Ain as a finished work. The Ain was completed in 1598. Which judgement about the register's date is soundest?

options.text_md: It was written in 1598, the year the Ain was completed
It was written before 1598, since the Ain describes methods that were already in use
It cannot be dated, since it names no year
It was written after 1598, though the register alone does not show how long after

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** It was written after 1598, though the register alone does not show how long after. Referring to a finished work sets an earliest date. Nothing in the register sets a latest date, and nothing ties it to the year of completion.

questions.stem_md: Two imagined accounts of the land classes of a province give the same figures and the same odd error in adding them up. A historian finds that the second writer, a clerk, copied from the Ain-i Akbari. How should she treat the second account?

options.text_md: As a second confirmation of the figures
As proof that the Ain's figures were checked against the villages
As proof that both writers invented the figures
As adding nothing independent, since it repeats the Ain and its error; she should look for records made from village measurement

Compare scale and purpose: the Ain sums up a whole province over both seasons, while one register covers a single village, so they need not conflict; check whether the village was typical
